title: Debugging & Logic
sources: Python Automation Engineer Handbook (complete edition, Oct 2026)

challenges.title: Three retries, two attempts
challenges.description: A connectivity check is supposed to try up to three times, but logs show only two attempts.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: range's stop value is excluded.
List what range(1, 3) produces.
challenges.explanation:
range(1, 3) yields 1 and 2. Use range(1, max_retries + 1) or range(max_retries) to get three attempts.
        Off-by-one errors at loop bounds are among the most common automation bugs.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 6 Loops
options: ping() must be called before the loop
max_retries must be a string
break exits the loop too late
range(1, max_retries) stops before 3, so only attempts 1 and 2 run

challenges.title: Build an error counter
challenges.description: Reassemble a function that counts ERROR lines in a log file.
challenges.instructions: Put the lines in an order that produces a working function. Indentation is shown.
hints: The counter must exist before the loop uses it.
return goes after the with block finishes.
challenges.explanation:
The counter is initialised, the file is opened with an explicit encoding, each line is checked, and the
            total is returned after the file is closed by the with block.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 12 File Handling; Project P3

challenges.title: The copy that was not a copy
challenges.description: A test copies a config dict before changing the BMC user.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: dict() makes a shallow copy.
The inner dict is shared by both outer dicts.
challenges.explanation:
dict(base) copies only the outer level; both dicts reference the same inner dict, so changing it through
            copy also changes base. Use copy.deepcopy(base) for nested configuration.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 20 Memory Management; Ch. 7 Data Structures

challenges.title: Status check that sometimes fails
challenges.description: This check passes in the REPL but fails intermittently when the status comes from a parsed response.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: Two equal strings are not necessarily the same object.
Which operator compares values?
challenges.explanation:
is checks whether both operands are the same object. Interned literals can make it look as if it works,
        but a string built at runtime is a different object. Python 3.8+ even warns: "is" with a literal.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 3 Operators; Ch. 39 B3
options: split() always returns one element
is compares identity, not value; use == for strings
strip() changes the case of the string
mark_passed() must be called before the if

challenges.title: Greedy regex
challenges.description: Extract the first component name in angle brackets.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: .+ matches as much as it can.
The final > in the pattern matches the last > in the text.
challenges.explanation:
.+ is greedy: it expands to the end and backtracks only as far as needed to find a >, which is the last
            one. Use the lazy form <(.+?)> or a negated class <([^>]+)> to stop at the first >.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 17 Regular Expressions
challenges.code:
import re
m = re.search(r"<(.+)>", "<fan1> stalled, <psu2> lost")
print(m.group(1))

verify.template:
import re
m = re.search(r"<(.+)>", "<fan1> stalled, <psu2> lost")
print(m.group(1))

challenges.title: BOOT OK never matches
challenges.description: The UART log clearly contains a line BOOT OK, yet this loop never reports success.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: Iterating a file yields lines with their line endings.
What does repr(line) show?
challenges.explanation:
Lines from a file keep their trailing "
" (and serial captures often have "
"). Compare
        line.strip() == "BOOT OK" or use line.rstrip("
").
challenges.source: Linux, Bash & Embedded Debugging Handbook · UART capture analysis; Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 12
options: The with block closes the file before the loop runs
Files must be read with f.read() before looping
String comparison is case-insensitive
Each line still ends with a newline character, so it never equals "BOOT OK"

challenges.title: Zero errors found?
challenges.description: A parser that searches for "ERROR" reports 0 errors, but the log contains lines like "error: i2c-3 timeout" and "Error: PSU2 lost".
challenges.instructions: What is the most likely cause?
hints: Compare the exact letters.
"error" != "ERROR"
challenges.explanation:
Substring checks are case-sensitive. Normalise with line.upper() or use re.search(r"\berror\b", line,
       re.IGNORECASE) when the log mixes capitalisations.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Project P3; Linux, Bash & Embedded Debugging Handbook · log analysis
options: The log is too large to parse
The file is opened in text mode
The search is case-sensitive
Python cannot search strings for substrings

challenges.title: The 20-minute timeout
challenges.description: A 60-second power-on wait occasionally runs for 20 minutes on lab machines that sync with NTP.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: What happens to the elapsed time if the clock jumps back?
Which clock is guaranteed never to go backwards?
challenges.explanation:
If NTP steps the clock backwards, time.time() - start shrinks and the deadline moves away. time.monotonic()
        is immune to clock changes and is the right choice for measuring durations.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 18; API & Protocol Automation Handbook Q24
options: time.sleep(2) is too short
The while condition is evaluated only once
TimeoutError cannot be raised manually
time.time() follows the wall clock, which NTP can step backwards; use time.monotonic()

challenges.title: Late-binding lambdas
challenges.description: A list of check callbacks is built in a loop.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: A lambda looks up i when it is called, not when it is created.
What is i after the loop finishes?
challenges.explanation:
Closures capture variables, not values. All three lambdas read i when called, after the loop has left
            it at 2. Bind the value with a default argument: lambda i=i: i * 10.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 19 Advanced Functions
challenges.code:
checks = [lambda: i * 10 for i in range(3)]
print([c() for c in checks])

verify.template:
checks = [lambda: i * 10 for i in range(3)]
print([c() for c in checks])

challenges.title: Bisect a regression
challenges.description: A sensor regression appeared somewhere between a known-good and a known-bad firmware build.
challenges.instructions: Order the steps of a binary search for the first bad build.
hints: You need two known endpoints before you can halve the range.
Each test halves the remaining range.
challenges.explanation:
Binary search needs a good and a bad endpoint, then repeatedly tests the midpoint and moves one boundary.
            With N candidate builds it needs about log2(N) tests. git bisect automates exactly this for commits.
challenges.source: Git, Jenkins & CI/CD Handbook · Ch. 5 Git Troubleshooting (git bisect)
steps: Mark the newest failing build as bad and an older passing build as good
Test the build halfway between good and bad
If it fails it becomes the new bad, otherwise it becomes the new good
Repeat until the good and bad builds are adjacent
Report the bad build of the adjacent pair as the first bad build

challenges.title: Floor division and banker's rounding
challenges.description: Compute buffer pages and display rounded values.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: // rounds towards negative infinity.
round() uses round-half-to-even.
challenges.explanation:
Floor division always rounds down, so -7 // 2 is -4, not -3. round() rounds halves to the nearest even
            integer, so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 3 Operators

challenges.title: Lost updates across threads
challenges.description: Eight threads each call record_pass() 10,000 times, yet the final count is sometimes below 80,000.
challenges.instructions: What is the root cause?
hints: += reads the value, adds one and writes it back.
Another thread can run between the read and the write.
challenges.explanation:
Even with the GIL, a thread switch can happen between loading passed and storing the new value, so two
        threads can write the same result. Guard the update with a Lock, or have each thread count locally and
        combine the totals.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 21 Concurrency and Parallelism; Project P11
challenges.code:
passed = 0

def record_pass():
    global passed
    passed += 1
options: passed += 1 is a read-modify-write that is not atomic; protect it with a threading.Lock
global variables cannot be used from threads
The GIL guarantees += is atomic, so the threads must be crashing
Integers overflow after 65,535

challenges.title: Mutating a dict while iterating
challenges.description: A loop adds keys to the dict it is iterating over.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Dicts detect size changes during iteration.
The exception message describes exactly what happened.
challenges.explanation:
Adding a key changes the dict's size, and the iterator raises RuntimeError on its next step. Iterate over a
            copy, for example for k in list(d):, when you need to modify the dict.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures; Ch. 36 Debugging
acceptedAnswers: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

verify.expectedOutput: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration

challenges.title: Passes alone, fails in the suite
challenges.description: test_fan_curve passes when run alone but fails when the whole suite runs.
challenges.instructions: Which cause is the most likely?
hints: What differs between the two runs?
Earlier tests run first only in the suite run.
challenges.explanation:
Order-dependent failures nearly always mean shared state: a module-level variable, a temp file, an
       environment variable or a device setting changed by an earlier test. Reset state in fixtures, and run the
       suite in random order (for example with the pytest-randomly plugin) to expose hidden dependencies.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 25 pytest; Ch. 37 Code Quality
options: Another test leaves shared state behind (globals, files, device settings)
Assertions are disabled in suite runs
The test file name is too long
pytest runs tests too quickly

challenges.title: Parse key=value pairs
challenges.description: A firmware banner prints space-separated key=value pairs; values may contain dots but not spaces.
challenges.instructions: Write one expression that turns the string line into a dict. Use dict() with a generator expression, the loop variable pair, and split("=", 1).
hints: line.split() with no argument splits on any whitespace.
dict() accepts an iterable of 2-item sequences.
challenges.explanation:
line.split() produces the pairs; pair.split("=", 1) splits each at the first = only, giving a 2-item list
           that dict() uses as key and value. maxsplit=1 keeps any later = characters in the value.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 9 Comprehensions; Ch. 42 Coding Interview Practice

challenges.title: Floating-point equality
challenges.description: A power calculation compares floats.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in binary.
Compare with a tolerance instead.
challenges.explanation:
0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, so == fails. Compare with a tolerance: math.isclose, an
            absolute bound, or pytest.approx in tests.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 2 Data Types; Ch. 25 pytest (approx)

challenges.title: The loop that never ends
challenges.description: When check() keeps failing, this retry loop runs forever instead of stopping after three tries.
challenges.instructions: What is the bug?
hints: Look at the indentation of the last line.
Which statements belong to the while body?
challenges.explanation:
In Python, indentation defines the block. retries += 1 runs only after the loop ends, so inside the loop
        retries stays 0 forever. Indent it to the loop body level.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 6 Loops; Ch. 36 Debugging
options: retries += 1 is outside the loop body because of its indentation
break should be continue
while loops cannot use <
check() must return a string

challenges.title: Find the first bad build
challenges.description: Reassemble a binary-search helper that returns the first failing build from an ordered list.
challenges.instructions: Put the lines in an order that produces a correct function. Indentation is shown.
hints: The bounds must exist before the loop.
If mid is bad, the first bad build is at mid or earlier.
challenges.explanation:
When the midpoint is bad, the answer is at mid or before it, so hi = mid. When it is good, the answer is
            after it, so lo = mid + 1. The loop ends when lo == hi, which is the first bad build (assuming the last
            build is bad).
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 35 Data Structures, Algorithms and Coding Interviews

challenges.title: Natural version order
challenges.description: Sort firmware build names.
challenges.instructions: Type exactly what this program prints. Each print() call is one line.
hints: Strings sort character by character.
The key converts the number part to an int.
challenges.explanation:
Without a key, "fw10" sorts before "fw2" because "1" < "2". Converting the numeric part to int gives
            numeric order. The same trap appears when comparing version strings.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 7 Data Structures
challenges.code:
builds = ["fw10", "fw9", "fw2"]
print(sorted(builds), sorted(builds, key=lambda s: int(s[2:])))

verify.template:
builds = ["fw10", "fw9", "fw2"]
print(sorted(builds), sorted(builds, key=lambda s: int(s[2:])))

challenges.title: The slow allow-list
challenges.description: A script checks 50,000 serial numbers against an allow-list of 20,000 entries stored in a Python list. It takes minutes.
challenges.instructions: Which change gives the biggest speed-up?
hints: How expensive is x in some_list?
Which structure has O(1) membership tests?
challenges.explanation:
x in list scans the list, so the job is about 50,000 × 20,000 comparisons. A set uses hashing, making each
       membership test O(1) on average and the whole job roughly 50,000 operations.
challenges.source: Python Automation Engineer Handbook · Ch. 20 Memory Management and Performance; Ch. 35
options: Print fewer log messages
Use a while loop instead of a for loop
Convert the allow-list to a set before the loop
Sort the 50,000 serial numbers first
